notes.text:
I'm planning test drops at several altitudes, since wind measured at each height gives the shear and veer directly. I'd release them away from the smoke to avoid updraft, but they still drift, so the release point has to stay within 500 m of the origin. After that I'd add a few drops through the smoke to measure the updraft.

I'm setting up test drops at altitudes of 150, 100, 50, and 30 m, placed upwind of the fire at around (-300, 0), and I'll check whether the wind pushes them into the smoke. I'm also considering a starting speed of 45 and a heading of 90.

I'm estimating the wind speed at 100 m as about 10.7 toward roughly 206°, then working out the shear exponent from the ratios at 50 m and 150 m, which comes out to about 0.3. I'm also checking the veer between heights, which looks small, somewhere around 0 to 4 degrees over that span.

I'm checking the veer estimates against the 50 m and 150 m readings, which suggests roughly 7 degrees per 100 m with some noise around 4 degrees, so I'll refine that later. I'm also noting that a 100 m fall takes about 7 seconds, well above the 4.5 seconds of free fall, so drag is significant and I should account for it before working out where to release the drop upwind of the fire.
Longer predicted fall times suggest the drag is too small, so I'll raise it and try 0.035.
The drag went the wrong way: the timestep grew once I added more drag, which makes sense. So I'll lower the drag and try 0.025.

I'm interpolating the dt values between 0.03 and 0.025 to find where they cross zero, which looks to be around 0.0275. The dy values give a zero near 0.0281, so I'm going to try 0.028. Test 3 still doesn't match quite right, and I suspect the wind speed at 50 might be the cause.

Next I'm adding the updraft and tuning the veer and speed; aircraft speed matters in the mix, not drag. I'll test low drops at 30 to 50 meters through the fire center at different speeds, and model the updraft as a vertical velocity that falls off with distance from center, which lengthens fall time. I'm also looking at a 150-meter drop through the center to see how much more time the payload spends in the updraft.

I'm going to simulate a drop at altitude 100 with the aircraft heading 206 at speed 45, then work out the release point that puts the impact at the center by offsetting by the displacement I get.

I'm checking that the smoke starts at the center, then setting the release point at (54.9, 114.1) with heading 206, speed 45, and altitude 100. The trajectory ends up passing through the center, which works. I'll also try versions at altitude 150 and maybe a low altitude, starting with the first.

I'm comparing the observed fall of 7.40 against the predicted 7.05 with no updraft, which suggests the impact landed a bit short. The impact point sits at (-2.9, -5.5) rather than at the target (0, 0), so it's displaced by about 5.5 in y. I think the updraft slowed the fall, so I'll check it against the updraft values.

I'm weighing whether the updraft of about 3 still fits, given the 198° wind reading at 100 m, which is a notable discrepancy. I'll add more drops that are sensitive to low-altitude lingering, since the updraft's effect should grow with time spent in the column. I plan to test a 150 m drop and a 40 m drop through the center, and simulate offsets for each under the current updraft-3 hypothesis.

I'm checking the smoke start: the updraft acts early, so releasing from the center won't do. Starting the load offset outside the smoke, the point at (72.3, 147.5) works for the 150 case, sitting about 164 from center, and (36.1, 75.6) works for the 40 case at distance 84.

I'm checking the sign of the predicted-minus-observed vertical difference, which tells me whether the prediction landed too far north or south. The observed drop was about 5.5 units farther south than predicted, and an updraft should lengthen the fall and push the drift south, so I'm testing whether that explains the gap.

I'm checking whether a stronger updraft, maybe 4 instead of 3, would account for the southward mismatch, since the smoke tests all use heading 206 while the non-smoke ones show almost no vertical difference.

Updraft looks like it's closer to 2.5 to 3 now, since the fit gets worse when I push it higher. The y residual in test 6 is still sitting around 5 to 6 and isn't going away. At 40 m the wind speed checks out: the power-law model gives about 8.1, matching the measured value. The direction is off by a little, though, since the model gives roughly 204 against a measured 201, which is close to where test 3 landed at 50 m.

Checking the wind direction across tests now: test 4 at 100 m reads 198, test 1 reads 206, and tests 2 and 5 at 150 m read 208 and 203. With about 4° of noise, I'm trying a wind direction near 202 with a small veer, then testing whether a 4° rotation would shift test 1 enough to matter.

I'm going back to heading 206 after the dx got worse, and I'm trying more shear and speed variants to fix the dy residuals in tests 4 through 6. Since those aircraft move along 206 at speed 45, I'm wondering whether the along-track drag is off, and I'm considering raising wind_speed a bit.

Weighing the sign of the dy residual against the drag and wind trade-off: lower drag lets flights on heading 206 travel further north, so more wind to the south would offset that. I'm settling on trying drag 0.026 with wind_speed 11.3.

I'm weighing whether the fit is good enough: with a 3 m mean error the score would be about 0.5, but I want something better. The four remaining test drops should mimic operating conditions, though I don't know the targets yet, and the constraints might call for different headings or speeds, so I can't run them just yet.

I'm picking the last four test drops to look like real operating conditions, since the targets aren't known yet, spanning high and low speeds and altitudes plus several headings. Outside the smoke is mostly better for refining wind and drag, and one drop inside the smoke at a different speed would add coverage. I'm sketching positions for each: one heading east at 80 m/s and 150 m altitude, one heading west at 80 m/s from 30 m, one heading south at 60 m/s from 120 m, and one heading northwest at 70 m/s from 70 m.

I'm comparing the test 7 residual: the predicted eastward travel came out shorter than observed, so I'm weighing whether drag at high speed or a weaker wind component is causing the gap.

I'm checking the other residuals for the same pattern: the model seems to undershoot travel along the heading, so I'll try a lower drag with a stronger wind and compare against all the tests.

I'm seeing that the high-altitude fall times come out too short, so my drag estimate is too low for those cases. Between the values I tried, the best fit looks to be around 0.027. I'm also wondering whether the low-altitude result, which sits at 0.08 with the 0.0279 setting, points to a lower value still, and I'm weighing how wind shear aloft might matter, though fall time should depend only on vertical drag.

I'm settling on a drag of 0.027 with a wind of 11.0, shear of 0.3, and updraft of 3 to run next.

I'm checking the three test points at 150 m, where the predictions land too far west, and I'm wondering whether the wind direction there needs to veer. The measured values at 150 m average about 205, while the other altitudes hover around 200 to 203, so the overall mean sits near 203.

Now I'm weighing whether the wind at 150 m should come from a more southerly direction, since the model puts it at 207.5. Veering it negative would shift the direction, but an earlier test with a higher veer made the x-error worse everywhere. I'm considering less shear instead, which would reduce the westward drift at that height, and I'll test a flat veer of 0 with direction 205 next.

Test 5 and test 6 are drifting in y by about +5, which stands out against test 4, which is fine. Since these are smoke tests, I'm wondering whether the updraft model is off, maybe stronger but with lower drag, though dt seems to fit. I'm also considering the observation noise of 1.5 on each axis as an alternative explanation.

I'm checking whether tests 5 and 6 are drifting because of the updraft: the updraft might slow the fall and give the wind more time to push the load south. But dt matches, so that probably isn't it. I'll try a stronger updraft with a bit less drag and see which tests improve.

The estimate hasn't settled anything yet, so I'm weighing whether to use the last test drop or run an off-center smoke drop to check the radial profile. The updraft model is taken as given. My working values are drag 0.027, wind speed 11.0, direction 206, shear 0.3, veer 0, and updraft 3. The negative dx residuals suggest the predictions lean too far west, so I'm considering nudging the wind direction toward the south, toward 180.

I'm checking the wind direction: the dx residuals average around -2, so the predictions lean too far west. I'm considering moving the direction to 204 with a small veer of 3, which would bring it closer to the south.
I'm tuning the direction and shear so the high-altitude drift moves back east. The 150 m tests drift too far west, so I'll try a direction near 203 with a slight positive veer and lower shear.

I'm checking whether test 6 still holds at dy 4.7, and wondering if the updraft is stronger at low altitude. I'm considering using a final test to probe low altitude with smoke at a different speed, since the operation likely drops at various heights. I'll try altitude 30, speed 80, heading 26 against the wind, or alternatively heading 90 at speed 70 and altitude 60.

I'm weighing the wind-heading option and a faster drop as the final test, and I'd run the simulation to pick the release point under the current hypothesis.

I'm working out the release point: shifting the target by that offset puts the drop at (-63.7, 31.1). The load passes through smoke, but the entry point is outside the cloud at radius 71, and the trajectory still ends at the center, so this works.
Test 10 checks out, with the predicted fall of 5.47 close to the observed 5.52. That's good enough, so I'm starting operation.

I'm planning each target by picking mid-range parameters and simulating the impact of a release at that target, then correcting the release point by the displacement. I'm also wondering whether the simulate tool's updraft figure, which is for fire intensity 1, scales with the real fire, or whether it only models the calibration fire at the origin, since the tool description says it knows nothing about the real air.

I'm wondering whether the simulate tool models the fire at the origin only, so I could test with updraft set to 0 first for the displacement, then check at the real location whether the updraft makes a difference. The intensity scaling and radius mismatch are the harder part, so I'll need to approximate.

I've confirmed the simulation does track the targets' fires, since the smoke entry flag changes the fall time. Next I'll shift the release point by the wind displacement from the 3.2 updraft, then check whether the release start falls inside the smoke column.

I'm still checking how the updraft shifts the release point, and the sensitivity looks small enough that the result holds. Next I'll run the simulation from the new release point at (-946, 544.4).
I'm off by about (-1.6, -3.1), so I'll adjust the release point to roughly (-944.4, 547.5) to correct for that. The path shifts a little with that change, so I'll need to simulate it again.

The fall time with the updraft comes out at 7.22 seconds against 6.1 without it, so the updraft's effect is large; its peak of about 4.4 m/s is driven by the intensity setting. The impact positions barely shift, which seems acceptable, so I'll move on.
Target 2: heading 115, alt 93, speed 52.

The second attempt was wasted because I used the wrong parameters for target 3, so I'm moving on. Now I'm on target 2, with a displacement of +45.2 and -78.6. The release values are -871.2 and -1617.4.
I'm checking whether the measurement is within half a metre, and a slightly smaller value counts as fine, so I'm dropping it.
I'm looking at the displacement values, +44.6 and +13.2, alongside the release coordinates at 1358.4 and 1158.8.
I'm applying a small offset to the release point, nudging it by about +0.8 and +1.7, which brings it to roughly (1359.2, 1160.5). That position looks right.
I'm checking the two disparity vectors against their release positions: T4 moves from (+41, +17.8) to (-381, 1066.2), and T5 from (+49.3, -26.3) to (1819.7, -63.7).
I'm adjusting the T4 target to (-380.5, 1067.4) from a want of (+0.5, +1.2), and shifting T5 to (1821.8, -60.4) from (+2.1, +3.3).
